To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the adipocyte-derived hormone, adiponectin, can be a therapeutic target for obesity-related heart disease, including obesity-associated cardiomyopathy.

(1) adiponectin deficiency exacerbates obesity cardiomyopathy; (2) adiponectins anti-oxidant and anti-inflammatory properties protect against obesity cardiomyopathy by attenuating the activation of NF-κB; (3) adiponectis anti-apoptotic properties protect against obesity-induced cardiomyocyte death by attenuating the expression of pro-apoptotic genes; (4) adiponectimimetic therapy with the synthetic adiponectin receptor agonist
the adipocyte-derived hormone leptin, which is elevated in obesity, is able to activate the RAS in cardiomyocytes, and this leads to the development of obesity cardiomyopathy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of molecular pathways and targets that can be used to prevent and treat obesity cardiomyopathy.
understanding the mechanisms that contribute to obesity cardiomyopathy.
the identification of novel targets and pathways for the prevention and/or treatment of obesity-associated cardiomyopathy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
obesity cardiomyopathy is a complex disease that involves a myriad of molecular, cellular, and physiological alterations, many of which are interdependent.
obesity is a major risk factor for the development of cardiovascular disease, which can manifest as a non-ischemic form of heart disease, known as obesity cardiomyopathy.
obesity cardiomyopathy is a multifactorial disease, which is not well understood, and which requires a multi-disciplinary approach to elucidate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
obesity cardiomyopathy can be viewed as a metabolic disease.

the obesity-associated co-mor-bidities are a consequence of a complex network of molecular events, and that the development of obesity cardiomyopathy is a consequence of a combination of metabolic, inflammatory, and mechanical stressors.

the metabolic syndrome and obesity are associated with the activation of a variety of pathways that are detrimental to the heart, including the ER-stress response, mitochondrial dysfunction, autophagy and inflammation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
obesity cardiomyopathy is an important and underappreciated complication of obesity, and that it is a major contributing factor in the increased risk of heart disease in obese subjects.
the obesity-induced increase in the expression and activity of SGLT2 is likely an important contributor to the pathogenesis of obesity cardiomyopathy.
the ER stress response is a major contributor to obesity cardiomyopathy.
